1.why: The recovery token is stored inside the requesting session's server-side state (state.recovery) and verified only against that session, so a code is implicitly bound to its requester, though binding is to a session rather than a real account record.

2.why: Tokens live only in the issuing session's server-side state, so another session/browser has state.recovery === undefined and any token submitted there fails verification.

3.why: The reset-password handler only overwrites protectedAccount.passwordHash and flips session flags; it never deletes or invalidates other entries in the global sessions map, so pre-existing sessions remain valid until their TTL expires.

4.why: Bun.serve is configured with TLS-only (cert/key), non-HTTPS requests are rejected, and HSTS is set, but no minimum/latest TLS version is explicitly pinned — it relies on Bun defaults with a local self-signed cert.

5.why: Passwords are hashed with bcrypt (cost 10), but the recovery token and MFA code are held in cleartext in memory (state.recovery.token, MFA_TEST_CODE) and returned in cleartext in JSON responses — no encryption or hashing of reset codes.

6.why: There is no email delivery at all; instead the 'mockDeliveryToken' and 'mockRecoveryLink' are returned directly in the API response and echoed into the client log panel, so nothing is hidden or guarded in a message.

7.why: Input is strictly validated (validAccountIdentifier regex, passwordPolicy, JSON object type checks, maxLength on fields) and never reflected into HTML — the client uses only textContent/createElement.

8.why: Navigation uses same-origin history.pushState with an allowlisted set of view names, the 'token' query param is regex-checked, and CSP sets form-action 'self' and base-uri 'none' — no external or user-controlled redirects exist.

9.why: No email templates exist, but every message shown is static text inserted via textContent with a nonce-based CSP forbidding inline/untrusted scripts, so no user-supplied HTML or script can appear in any generated message.

10.why: The client explicitly logs secrets — log("Mock recovery delivery token: " + token), the recovery link, and log("Mock MFA verification code: " + result.mockMfaCode) — to the console and the visible #log-list panel.

11.why: Passwords are bcrypt-hashed, but the shared verification secret MFA_TEST_CODE = "246810" and the recovery identifier MOCK_RECOVERY_SCENARIO are hardcoded constants in the source rather than configuration/secret storage.

12.why: A fixed, hardcoded MFA code ("246810") and a fixed known recovery identifier ("local-recovery-demo") act as default credentials that always work for anyone who reads or guesses them.

13.why: Both token verification and MFA verification use registerFailure/blocked with MAX_FAILURES = 5 and a 60-second lockout returning HTTP 429, though the counters are per-session and reset by obtaining a fresh session cookie.

14.why: The generic message is identical for all inputs, but when the identifier matches the mock scenario the response additionally contains mockDeliveryToken/mockRecoveryLink, which distinguishes a recoverable account from a non-existent one.

15.why: randomValue(32) uses crypto.getRandomValues to produce a 32-byte base64url token, valid for 10 minutes, single-use (recovery.used), compared in constant time, and scoped to the requesting session.
